Quotas and throttling are applied on a best-effort basis, and API keys identify callers rather than authenticate them, so combine them with an authorizer (IAM, Amazon Cognito or a Lambda authorizer).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Lambda counting in memory:** Lambda execution environments are created and discarded independently, so in-memory counters are not shared across concurrent instances and are lost when environments end.
- ✗ **B. S3 bucket policy by IP:** bucket policies control access to S3 objects; they cannot count or limit calls to a GenAI API.
- ✗ **C. CloudWatch dashboard:** a dashboard only displays request volumes; it does not stop a partner once the limit is reached.
- ✓ **D. Usage plans with per-partner API keys (correct):** a usage plan enforces a daily request quota for each key, which is exactly a 10,000-requests-per-day limit per partner without custom code.

## Key idea
Enforce per-partner request quotas with API Gateway usage plans and API keys; dashboards and in-memory counters cannot enforce limits.
Q002957:
## Content filters in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
Guardrail **content filters** detect harmful content in categories: hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct, plus a prompt attack filter.
- Each category has a filter strength of none, low, medium or high, set **separately for inputs (prompts) and outputs (responses)**.
- A higher strength blocks content even when the classifier's confidence is lower, so **high** blocks the most, including milder cases.
- When a filter triggers, the guardrail returns your configured blocked message instead of the prompt reaching the model or the response reaching the user.
Example for a children's app: sexual = high on input and high on output, so an inappropriate question is stopped before the model sees it, and any unsuitable generated text is replaced before display.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Sexual content filter at high on inputs and outputs (correct):** the guardrail enforces the policy on both directions at the strictest strength, independent of how the model behaves.
- ✗ **B. Polite system prompt:** instructions are a request the model may not always follow, and they can be overridden by jailbreaks; nothing checks the prompt or response.
- ✗ **C. Contextual grounding relevance threshold:** grounding checks judge whether an answer is supported by the source and relevant to the question; they do not detect sexual content.
- ✗ **D. Short word list:** a few listed words miss synonyms, misspellings and context, so most inappropriate content would pass.

## Key idea
Strict category blocking in both directions comes from guardrail content filters set to high on inputs and outputs, not from prompts, grounding checks or short word lists.
Q002958:
## Amazon Bedrock data handling
Amazon Bedrock is designed so customer data stays under the customer's control:
- Prompts and completions are **not used to train** the base foundation models and are **not shared with the model providers**. Model providers have no access to the deployment accounts where models run.
- Bedrock does not store prompts and responses by default; storing them requires you to enable **model invocation logging** to your own CloudWatch Logs or S3.
- Inference runs in the Region you call. **Cross-Region inference** profiles, if you choose them, can route requests to other Regions within a defined geography (or globally for global profiles) to gain throughput.
- Fine-tuning creates a private copy of the model that only your account can use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Shared with providers unless you pay to opt out:** Bedrock never shares prompts with providers for training, and there is no paid opt-out because it is the default for everyone.
- ✓ **B. (correct):** No training on prompts, in-Region unless cross-Region inference: this matches how Bedrock handles data; the only way requests leave the chosen Region is by opting into a cross-Region inference profile.
- ✗ **C. Stored permanently in one global location:** Bedrock does not keep prompts by default, and any logs you enable go to storage in your own account and chosen Region.
- ✗ **D. Sent to every Region automatically:** requests are processed in the Region you call; routing to other Regions happens only when a cross-Region inference profile is used, and even then only to a defined set of Regions.

## Key idea
Bedrock does not train on or share customer prompts, and data stays in the calling Region unless you opt into cross-Region inference.
Q002959:
## Functional versus non-functional requirements
A **functional** requirement says what the system does: summarize a ticket, draft a reply. A **non-functional** requirement says how well: latency, throughput, availability, cost and security.
For a goal like "cut support handling time by 30%", the assistant only helps if it responds fast enough while agents are working, including at the busiest hours.
- **Latency target**, for example p90 time to first token under 1 second and full reply under 4 seconds.
- **Throughput target**, for example 200 concurrent agents and 50 requests per second at peak.
These numbers drive architecture choices: model size, streaming, caching, on-demand versus provisioned throughput or cross-Region inference, quotas to request, and cost estimates.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Date of the all-hands meeting:** a meeting date is a scheduling detail with no effect on how the system must be designed or perform.
- ✗ **B. Chat widget color:** the color is a cosmetic UI choice; it does not influence models, capacity or response time.
- ✓ **C. Latency and throughput at peak (correct):** if replies are slow or throttled when support volume peaks, handling time does not fall, so these targets directly shape model choice, capacity and cost.
- ✗ **D. Names of first testers:** who tests the feature is a rollout detail, not a property the architecture has to meet.

## Key idea
Business goals such as faster handling translate into measurable latency and throughput targets under peak load, and those targets shape the architecture.
Q002960:
## Logging GenAI interactions for legal retention
Regulated firms often must keep records of what was asked and answered, for years, and hand them over on request (eDiscovery). That puts three demands on the log store:
- **Durable**: records survive for the full retention period, for example by writing them to Amazon S3 with lifecycle rules that move old objects to cheaper storage classes such as S3 Glacier.
- **Tamper-resistant**: nobody, including administrators, can change or delete records early. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode enforces this write-once-read-many (WORM) behavior.
- **Searchable**: records carry metadata (user, timestamp, model ID, application) so a legal team can find one customer's conversations quickly, for example by querying S3 with Amazon Athena.
## Where the data comes from
Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging can deliver full request and response bodies plus metadata to S3 or CloudWatch Logs. AWS CloudTrail adds who called which API, but it does not record the prompt and response text.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Developers' laptops:** laptops are not governed, backed-up or access-controlled storage. Data can be lost, altered or leaked, and nobody can prove the records are complete.
- ✗ **B. In-memory session storage:** memory is cleared on restart and only holds recent sessions, so nothing would exist to produce years later.
- ✗ **C. Aggregate token counts:** a daily token total says nothing about what was asked or answered, so it cannot satisfy a request for the actual interactions.
- ✓ **D. Durable, searchable, tamper-resistant storage (correct):** seven-year retention needs durable storage, legal requests need search over metadata, and evidence must be provably unaltered. Capturing full prompts, responses and metadata in immutable storage meets all three.

## Key idea
Legal retention needs the full prompts and responses kept durably, immutably and searchably; usage metrics or temporary storage cannot reproduce a conversation.
Q002961:
## Balancing cost and latency by workload
Model choice is a trade-off between quality, cost per token and latency. When quality is equal, the deciding factor is what the workload actually needs.
- **Interactive workloads** (chat, autocomplete) have a user waiting, so time to first token and total response time matter a lot.
- **Offline workloads** (overnight reports, bulk summarization) only need to finish within a window, such as before 7 a.m. Doubling the per-request latency rarely matters if the batch still completes in time.
## Example
Generating 10,000 reports overnight: if the cheaper model takes 8 seconds per report instead of 4 but runs with enough parallelism, the job still finishes in the window and the token bill is halved. For this kind of job, Amazon Bedrock batch inference can reduce cost further for supported models.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Latency always wins:** latency is critical only when a user or downstream system is waiting. For scheduled overnight jobs, paying twice as much for speed nobody notices wastes money.
- ✗ **B. Equal quality means identical models:** two models can score the same on an evaluation yet differ in price, speed, context window and behavior. Equal scores do not make the choice meaningless.
- ✗ **C. Send every report to both:** this doubles the cost with no quality gain, because both models already score the same.
- ✓ **D. Cheaper model for overnight work (correct):** quality is equal and nobody is waiting for each response, so lower cost per token is the benefit that matters; the extra latency only has to fit the batch window.

## Key idea
Match the model to the workload: for offline batch jobs at equal quality, choose the cheaper model, and pay for low latency only when someone is waiting.
Q002962:
## Ways to customize a model in Amazon Bedrock
- **Prompt engineering**: instructions and examples in the prompt. Cheapest and fastest, but some behaviors stay inconsistent.
- **Fine-tuning**: supervised training on labeled prompt-and-response pairs (JSONL files in S3). The model learns a specific task, format or style from the examples.
- **Continued pre-training**: training on large amounts of unlabeled text so the model absorbs domain knowledge and vocabulary. It does not teach a particular output format.
## When fine-tuning fits
Fine-tuning is the next step when prompting cannot reliably produce the required behavior and good labeled examples exist. For instance, 3,000 pairs of input and correctly formatted output teach the model the exact tone and structure. The result is a custom model you invoke instead of the base model.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Longer system prompt without examples:** prompting has already failed to give reliable results, and removing examples makes the instructions even less concrete.
- ✗ **B. Higher temperature:** temperature adds randomness to token choice, so outputs become less consistent, the opposite of enforcing one style.
- ✓ **C. Fine-tuning with labeled examples (correct):** the 3,000 high-quality examples show exactly the desired output for given inputs, which is what supervised fine-tuning needs to make a specific style consistent.
- ✗ **D. Continued pre-training on web data:** continued pre-training uses unlabeled text to add domain knowledge, and generic web data would not teach the organization's specific output style.

## Key idea
Labeled examples plus a need for consistent behavior points to fine-tuning; continued pre-training on unlabeled text adds knowledge, not a specific style.
Q002963:
## The Amazon Bedrock playgrounds
The Bedrock console includes playgrounds (chat, text and image) for trying models without writing code.
- Choose a model, type a prompt and see the response immediately.
- Adjust inference parameters such as temperature, top P and maximum output length, then rerun the same prompt to see the effect.
- Compare mode in the chat playground shows several models or configurations side by side.
## Example
A team wants to know whether temperature 0.2 or 0.8 gives better product descriptions. In the playground they run the same prompt at both settings in a minute and see the difference, before any SDK code, IAM role or pipeline exists.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Console playground (correct):** it is interactive and instant, with parameter controls built in, so the team can explore many settings in minutes without deploying anything.
- ✗ **B. Batch inference job per setting:** batch inference is an asynchronous job with input files in S3 for large volumes, meant for throughput, not quick back-and-forth experiments.
- ✗ **C. SageMaker endpoint per setting:** inference parameters are sent with each request, so no new endpoint is needed to change them; deploying endpoints adds cost and setup time for nothing.
- ✗ **D. Fine-tuned copy per setting:** fine-tuning changes model weights, while temperature and top P are request-time settings. Training jobs take hours and cost money for something a request parameter controls.

## Key idea
Inference parameters are request-time settings, so explore them interactively in the Bedrock playground rather than with jobs, endpoints or training.
Q002964:
## How metadata filters work in retrieval
Knowledge bases can store metadata with each chunk, for example from a `.metadata.json` sidecar file per document in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. At query time a filter narrows which chunks vector search may return.
Filters compare stored values literally. If one document stores `03/14/2025`, another `2025-03-14` and a third `14 Mar 2025`, no single filter matches them all correctly, and documents are wrongly included or excluded.
In Bedrock Knowledge Bases the range operators (`greaterThan`, `lessThan` and their "or equals" forms) compare numbers, so a date used in a range filter should be stored as a number.
## Fix it at the source
Normalize the values in the ingestion pipeline, before indexing:
- Convert every date to one consistent representation, for example a number such as `20250314` or epoch seconds, so range filters compare them correctly.
- Validate the metadata and reject or flag documents whose dates cannot be parsed.
Then re-sync so the index contains consistent values.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Disable metadata filters:** this hides the symptom by throwing away the feature; users then get results from any date, which is what the filters existed to prevent.
- ✓ **B. Normalize metadata in ingestion (correct):** the problem is inconsistent stored values, so fixing them once, before indexing, makes every later filter reliable without changing queries.
- ✗ **C. Ask users to type several formats:** the stored values stay inconsistent, and users cannot guess every format in the data, so matches remain incomplete.
- ✗ **D. Ask the model to interpret dates:** filtering happens in the retrieval step before the model sees anything, so the model cannot repair documents the filter already missed.

## Key idea
Metadata filters compare stored values literally, so normalize formats in the ingestion pipeline instead of working around them at query or prompt time.
Q002965:
## A gated ingestion pipeline
Before documents enter a knowledge base, a pipeline can check them and only pass the good ones on.
- Step 1: a document lands in a landing (raw) S3 bucket, which triggers an AWS Step Functions workflow.
- Step 2: validation tasks run, for example a Lambda function that checks the schema and required metadata, and a PII scan with Amazon Comprehend `DetectPiiEntities` or Amazon Macie.
- Step 3: a `Choice` state routes passing documents to the knowledge base source bucket and failing ones to a quarantine bucket, with a notification for reviewers.
## Why Step Functions
Step Functions gives each document a visible execution history, built-in retries and error handling, and clear branching. Reviewers can fix a quarantined document and resubmit it, and nothing sensitive reaches the index in the meantime.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Ingest everything, email a weekly summary:** documents with PII or bad schema are already indexed and retrievable for up to a week before anyone reads the summary.
- ✗ **B. Direct user uploads without checks:** nothing scans for PII or validates schema, so sensitive or malformed documents go straight into retrieval.
- ✓ **C. Step Functions with quarantine routing (correct):** validation runs before ingestion, only passing documents reach the knowledge base, and failures are kept in a separate bucket for human review.
- ✗ **D. Nightly deletion of failures:** deleting without review loses documents that may only need a small fix, and the requirement explicitly asks for quarantine and review.

## Key idea
Validate before indexing and route failures to quarantine for review, rather than ingesting first and fixing later or deleting outright.
Q002966:
## Vector search latency
Vector search finds the nearest neighbors of a query embedding among stored embeddings. Comparing against every vector is slow at millions of items, so engines build approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes such as HNSW, which walk a graph of vectors to find close matches quickly.
Where the index lives drives latency:
- **In-memory engines** keep the index in RAM. Amazon MemoryDB vector search offers single-digit millisecond query latency with high recall, even as updates arrive.
- **Disk or object storage** options trade some latency for lower cost and are fine when tens or hundreds of milliseconds are acceptable.
## Example
A real-time assistant with 5 million document chunks needs retrieval under 10 ms so the whole response stays fast; an in-memory HNSW index serves that, while scanning files does not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. In-memory vector search such as MemoryDB (correct):** the ANN index is held in memory, which gives very low query latency over millions of vectors, matching both requirements.
- ✗ **B. Precompute answers for every query:** users can ask an effectively unlimited number of different questions, so answers cannot be precomputed, and they would go stale as data changes.
- ✗ **C. Unindexed text columns:** embeddings stored as text cannot be compared by vector distance without parsing and scanning every row, which is far too slow for millions of vectors.
- ✗ **D. Athena over CSV files:** Athena scans files in S3 per query and typically takes seconds, and it has no vector index, so it cannot provide interactive similarity search.

## Key idea
For millisecond vector search over millions of items, use an in-memory ANN index; file scans and unindexed columns cannot meet that latency.
Q002967:
## What chunk overlap does
When a document is split into chunks, an idea can start at the end of one chunk and finish at the start of the next. Overlap repeats some text at each boundary so both chunks carry that context.
- Example: with 300-token chunks and 20% overlap, each chunk repeats about 60 tokens of the previous one.
- Benefit: a sentence cut at a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk, which improves retrieval of ideas that span boundaries.
- Cost: the repeated text is embedded and stored more than once, so the index grows and more tokens are sent to the model when overlapping chunks are both retrieved.
## In Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Fixed-size chunking has an `overlapPercentage` setting and hierarchical chunking an `overlapTokens` setting, while semantic chunking has no overlap setting; its `bufferSize` controls how many neighboring sentences are grouped when comparing meaning to find split points. Overlap is a tuning choice, not a rule.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Overlap reduces storage:** overlapping text is stored in every chunk that contains it, so storage increases, not decreases.
- ✓ **B. Context across boundaries, at a cost (correct):** overlap keeps boundary-spanning ideas retrievable, and the price is duplicated text, meaning more storage, embeddings and tokens.
- ✗ **C. Required for semantic, forbidden for fixed-size:** fixed-size chunking commonly uses overlap, and semantic chunking does not require it. Overlap is optional in both.
- ✗ **D. No effect on quality or size:** overlap directly changes the number of stored tokens and whether boundary-spanning ideas are retrieved intact.

## Key idea
Chunk overlap trades extra storage and tokens for better context at chunk boundaries; tune it rather than treating it as free or forbidden.
Q002968:
## How to tell chunking is wrong
Chunking decides which pieces of text become the units of retrieval. If chunk size or boundaries are poor, retrieval returns pieces that cannot answer the question even when the right document is found.
Typical symptoms:
- **Broken boundaries**: retrieved chunks end mid-sentence or split a table so the header row is in one chunk and the values in another.
- **Missing context**: the relevant chunk is found, but the fact it needs (for example which product a number refers to) is in a neighboring chunk.
## Possible fixes
- Increase chunk size or add overlap.
- Use semantic or hierarchical chunking so boundaries follow meaning, with small child chunks for matching and larger parent chunks for context.
- Use advanced parsing for tables and complex layouts, or a custom Lambda transformation for special formats.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Small font for chunk counts:** console display style has no effect on how documents are split or retrieved.
- ✗ **B. Uppercase bucket name:** S3 bucket names cannot contain uppercase letters anyway, and bucket naming has nothing to do with chunking quality.
- ✗ **C. Created on a Monday:** the creation date of a knowledge base has no influence on chunk boundaries or retrieval.
- ✓ **D. Chunks cut sentences or tables (correct):** boundaries that split meaningful units show the splitting rule ignores the structure of the content, a direct chunking problem.
- ✓ **E. Relevant chunks lack context (correct):** if the right chunk is retrieved but cannot answer on its own, chunks are too small or boundaries are badly placed.

## Key idea
Retrieved chunks that break sentences or tables, or that lack needed context, are the signals to revisit chunk size, overlap and strategy.
Q002969:
## Why phrasing affects retrieval
Retrieval embeds the user's question and searches for similar chunks. A vague, conversational or multi-part question ("what about the other one, and is it cheaper?") embeds poorly, so the best chunks may not be retrieved, and the answer suffers.
## Query reformulation
Before searching, a model rewrites the question into clearer search queries:
- Resolve references from the conversation, such as turning "the other one" into the product name.
- Expand abbreviations and add key terms.
- Split a complex question into sub-queries and retrieve for each.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports query decomposition in `RetrieveAndGenerate`, and custom pipelines can do the same with a small, fast model before calling `Retrieve`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Longer answers:** answer length is decided after retrieval; if the wrong chunks were retrieved, a longer answer only adds more unsupported text.
- ✗ **B. Higher temperature:** temperature affects how the model generates text, not which chunks the search returns, and it makes outputs less consistent.
- ✗ **C. Fewer documents in the index:** removing content reduces coverage, so some questions lose their only relevant source, and phrasing still affects matching.
- ✓ **D. Query reformulation (correct):** it turns differently phrased user questions into consistent, explicit search queries, so retrieval quality depends less on how the user wrote the question.

## Key idea
Fix phrasing sensitivity before the search by rewriting queries, not after retrieval by changing generation settings or shrinking the index.
Q002970:
## Stale versions in a knowledge base
If a data source holds `policy_v1.pdf`, `policy_v2.pdf` and `policy_v3.pdf`, all three are chunked and indexed. They are semantically similar, so a question about the policy can retrieve the outdated versions as readily as the current one.
Two complementary fixes:
- **Clean the source**: remove or archive superseded files and run a sync (ingestion job). Bedrock Knowledge Bases syncs incrementally and removes chunks of deleted files from the index.
- **Use metadata**: attach fields such as `version`, `status` or `effective_date` to each document. At query time, filter to `status = current` or rank newer documents higher.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Larger generation model:** the model answers from whatever chunks it is given; a larger model still receives the outdated chunks and has no reliable way to know they are stale.
- ✓ **B. Remove superseded versions and re-sync (correct):** after a sync, the stale chunks are no longer in the index, so they cannot be retrieved at all.
- ✗ **C. Increase top-k:** returning more results adds newer chunks but keeps the outdated ones too, so conflicting information still reaches the model.
- ✗ **D. Tell users to ignore outdated answers:** users usually cannot tell which answer is outdated, and it pushes a data quality problem onto them.
- ✓ **E. Filter or boost by version or date (correct):** metadata lets retrieval exclude old versions or prefer newer ones, which handles cases where old files must stay in the source.

## Key idea
Stale results are fixed at the data and retrieval layers, by removing old versions and filtering or ranking with version metadata, not by a bigger model or more results.
Q002971:
## Prompt templates for RAG
A RAG prompt template is a fixed prompt with placeholders filled in per request, for example:
- `Answer using only the passages below. If they do not contain the answer, say so.`
- `Passages: {{retrieved_passages}}`
- `Question: {{question}}`
The same template receives very different inputs over time: zero passages, one short passage, ten long ones, passages that conflict, or passages in a new format after the chunking strategy changes.
## Test with realistic, varied inputs
Keep an evaluation set that covers these cases and run the template against it whenever retrieval or the template changes. Check faithfulness to the passages, correct refusals when passages are irrelevant, and output format. Amazon Bedrock evaluations can score RAG responses for such metrics.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hard-coded sample passages:** every request would get the same passages regardless of the question, which defeats retrieval and gives wrong answers.
- ✗ **B. Assume it works without testing:** templates often fail on edge cases, such as empty or conflicting passages, and without tests those failures reach users.
- ✓ **C. Test against varied retrieval results (correct):** it verifies that the template behaves correctly across the real range of inputs it will receive, and catches regressions when retrieval changes.
- ✗ **D. Remove the placeholder and use web search:** foundation models do not search the web by themselves, and it would drop the company's own knowledge that RAG is meant to supply.

## Key idea
A RAG prompt template must be evaluated against the varied passages real retrieval produces, and retested whenever retrieval changes.
Q002972:
## Treating prompts like code
In production, a prompt is part of application behavior: one changed sentence can alter answers for every user. Prompts therefore need the same controls as code.
- **Versioning**: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management stores prompts with a working draft and immutable numbered versions, so applications can point at a tested version.
- **Access control**: IAM policies decide who may call actions such as `bedrock:UpdatePrompt` or `bedrock:CreatePromptVersion`, and on which prompt ARNs.
- **Approval**: a review step before promotion, such as a pull request review or a manual approval action in AWS CodePipeline, ensures someone checks and tests a new version before production uses it.
## Example
Teams edit drafts freely in development, but only a pipeline role can promote a version to production, and only after a reviewer approves it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. IAM restrictions on production prompts (correct):** only authorized roles can change what production uses, so ad hoc edits by any team are blocked.
- ✗ **B. Anyone may edit production directly:** this is the cause of the problem, as unreviewed changes go straight to users.
- ✗ **C. Store prompts in chat messages:** chat is not a controlled store, has no versions or permissions, and makes it unclear which text is actually in production.
- ✗ **D. Remove versioning:** without versions you cannot tell what changed, pin tested prompts or roll back a bad change.
- ✓ **E. Approval workflows before promotion (correct):** each new version is reviewed and tested before release, which directly stops unreviewed changes from reaching production.

## Key idea
Govern shared prompts with permissions on who can change production and an approval gate before a new version is promoted.
Q002973:
## Vague versus concrete instructions
Words like "concise", "short" or "detailed" mean different things to different readers, and a model interprets them differently from one request to the next. The result is inconsistent output.
Concrete instructions remove that ambiguity:
- Give a measurable limit: "Answer in at most three sentences" or "use no more than 50 words".
- Show the target format with an example (few-shot prompting), such as one sample question with a three-sentence answer.
- Optionally set the `maxTokens` inference parameter as a hard stop, remembering it truncates text rather than making the model plan a shorter answer.
## Example
"Be concise" might produce one line or three paragraphs; "Reply in exactly three sentences, like this example: ..." produces answers of nearly the same length every time.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Repeat "be concise":** repeating a vague word does not make it measurable, so the model still has to guess what concise means.
- ✓ **B. Concrete limit plus an example (correct):** a specific, measurable constraint and a demonstration tell the model exactly what length is expected, which makes length consistent.
- ✗ **C. Remove the instruction:** with no guidance, length depends entirely on the model and the question, so variation increases.
- ✗ **D. Raise the temperature:** higher temperature increases randomness in token choice, which makes length and wording less consistent, not more.

## Key idea
Replace vague adjectives with measurable constraints and an example; repetition or randomness does not make output consistent.
Q002974:
## Turning calls into RAG-ready text
Audio cannot be embedded for a text knowledge base directly; it first has to become text, and customer calls often contain names, card numbers and addresses.
- **Amazon Transcribe** converts speech to text. Its PII redaction feature finds personal data such as names, phone numbers and credit card numbers and replaces it in the transcript with a tag like `[PII]`. Transcribe Call Analytics adds speaker separation and call insights for contact center recordings.
- The redacted transcripts are then stored in S3, chunked and embedded into a knowledge base like any other document.
## The other language and media services
- Amazon Polly: text to speech (the reverse direction).
- Amazon Translate: text from one language to another text.
- Amazon Rekognition: analysis of images and video.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Rekognition on audio:** Rekognition analyzes images and video frames, for example objects, faces and text in images; it does not transcribe speech from audio files.
- ✗ **B. Polly to convert calls into text:** Polly turns text into lifelike speech, the opposite direction, so it cannot produce transcripts.
- ✓ **C. Transcribe with PII redaction, then chunk and embed (correct):** Transcribe is the AWS speech-to-text service and can redact PII during transcription, producing clean, searchable text ready for indexing.
- ✗ **D. Translate to convert audio to text:** Translate works on text input only; audio must be transcribed first, and it offers no PII redaction.

## Key idea
Speech to text with PII removal is Amazon Transcribe; Polly is text to speech, Translate is text to text, and Rekognition is for images and video.
Q002975:
## Choosing prompting, RAG or fine-tuning
Start with the simplest option and move on only when a real requirement demands it.
- **Prompting only**: the base model already knows enough and can already produce the behavior with good instructions and examples.
- **RAG**: answers depend on information the model never saw or that changes often, such as internal policies, product catalogs or yesterday's tickets. Retrieval supplies it at query time, and updating the knowledge base updates answers without retraining.
- **Fine-tuning**: the model must behave in a way prompting cannot reliably produce, such as a strict house style, a specialized output format or a narrow task.
## Example
A support bot that quotes current return policies needs RAG. A bot that must always answer in the company's legal drafting style may need fine-tuning. Both may be combined.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Private or changing information (correct):** this is the key test for RAG, since fine-tuned knowledge goes stale and retrieval keeps answers current and grounded in private data.
- ✗ **B. Chat color scheme:** user interface styling has no bearing on how the model gets knowledge or behavior.
- ✗ **C. Engineers' personal preferences:** technique choice should follow the use case's data and behavior needs, not taste.
- ✗ **D. Number of blog posts:** popularity does not show whether a technique fits this use case's data freshness or behavior requirements.
- ✓ **E. Style or behavior the base model cannot produce (correct):** this is the key test for fine-tuning, since knowledge gaps are better solved by retrieval but behavior gaps by training.

## Key idea
Missing or changing knowledge points to RAG; missing behavior or style points to fine-tuning; otherwise stay with prompting.
Q002976:
## Managed models versus self-hosted models
- **Amazon Bedrock** serves models as a managed service. You call an API and AWS runs the model; your VPC can reach it privately through an interface VPC endpoint, but the model runs in AWS-managed infrastructure and you do not control or download the provider's weights.
- **Self-hosting on Amazon SageMaker AI** means you deploy model weights you hold, such as an open-weight model, to endpoints you configure.
## How SageMaker keeps it inside your boundary
- Put the model's `VpcConfig` on your private subnets and security groups, so the endpoint's network interfaces live in your VPC.
- Store the weights in your own S3 bucket encrypted with your KMS key.
- Optionally enable network isolation so the container cannot make outbound calls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bedrock serverless without private networking:** the model runs in AWS-managed infrastructure with no control over weights, and without a VPC endpoint the traffic leaves the VPC through public endpoints.
- ✗ **B. Public third-party chatbot website:** data goes to an outside provider on the internet, and the company controls neither the model nor where it runs.
- ✗ **C. Another cloud's API over the internet:** requests leave the VPC across the public internet to infrastructure the company does not control, and the weights stay with that provider.
- ✓ **D. Open-weight model on SageMaker in the company VPC (correct):** the company holds the weights and the endpoint runs attached to its VPC, meeting both the network boundary and weight control requirements.

## Key idea
Full control over weights and a VPC-only boundary means self-hosting open weights on SageMaker in your VPC, not calling a managed or external API.
Q002977:
## Filtering versus boosting
- **Filtering** removes results that do not match a condition, such as `date >= 2025-01-01`. Older documents disappear completely, even when they are the only good answer.
- **Boosting** keeps every result but adjusts the ranking score, so newer documents move up while an old but highly relevant document can still appear.
## Example
In Amazon OpenSearch Service, a `function_score` query with a decay function (such as `gauss`) on a `published_date` field reduces the score of older documents gradually: a two-year-old document with a strong match can still outrank a new but weakly related one. The same idea can be done in application code by reranking retrieved results with a recency weight, which needs a date stored as metadata on each document.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Search only today's documents:** a hard filter to one day excludes nearly all content, which contradicts the requirement not to exclude older documents.
- ✗ **B. Ask the model to guess recency:** the model does not know document dates unless they are provided, and guessing happens after retrieval has already ranked the results.
- ✗ **C. Delete documents older than a month:** deletion permanently excludes older content, the opposite of keeping it available.
- ✓ **D. Boost with date metadata over the whole index (correct):** recent documents rank higher, and older relevant documents remain searchable, exactly matching "favor, not exclude".

## Key idea
To prefer recent content without losing older content, boost scores by a date field instead of filtering or deleting.
Q002978:
## Multi-tenant isolation for vector data
When several business units share one platform, each unit's data must be reachable only by its own users. Isolation is strongest when the data store enforces it, not only the application.
- **Separate index or collection per unit**: for example one Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection or index per unit, each with its own data access policy, or one Amazon Bedrock knowledge base per unit, with IAM policies naming each resource ARN.
- **Shared index with metadata filters**: cheaper, but a single bug that forgets the `business_unit` filter exposes everyone's data.
## Example
HR, Legal and Sales each get their own index. The HR application role is allowed only on the HR index, so even a faulty query cannot return Legal documents.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Single public index for all employees:** every employee could retrieve every unit's data, which breaks the different access policies.
- ✓ **B. Separate indexes or collections with access policies (correct):** each unit's vectors live in their own resource with its own permissions, so isolation is enforced by the data layer while the platform stays shared.
- ✗ **C. One file copied to each unit:** every unit would receive all vectors, including other units' data, and copies quickly drift out of sync.
- ✗ **D. Shared index with no metadata, application logic only:** with no metadata, the data cannot even be told apart, and any application bug exposes all units' data.

## Key idea
Enforce tenant isolation in the data layer with a separate index or collection and access policy per unit, not only in application code.
Q002979:
## Embeddings across languages
Retrieval works by comparing embeddings, which are vectors that place text with similar meaning close together. Whether this works across languages depends on the embeddings model.
- A **multilingual** model maps "refund policy" and "환불 정책" to nearby vectors, so a Korean question can find an English document and the reverse.
- An **English-only** model produces poor vectors for Korean text, so Korean documents and questions are matched badly.
Amazon Bedrock offers embeddings models built for multilingual text, such as Cohere Embed Multilingual. Check the model's documented language support and test retrieval with real questions in both languages.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Split the index by file size:** file size has nothing to do with language, so the language mismatch remains in every partition.
- ✗ **B. English-only model for speed:** it cannot represent Korean meaning well, so Korean questions and documents would retrieve poorly.
- ✓ **C. Embeddings model that supports both languages (correct):** the embeddings model decides whether English and Korean text with the same meaning land near each other, which is the basis of retrieval in both languages.
- ✗ **D. Translate everything and discard originals:** machine translation can lose nuance and terminology, and discarding originals removes the source text Korean users may need quoted.

## Key idea
For a mixed-language corpus and mixed-language questions, choose a multilingual embeddings model so meaning matches across languages.
Q002980:
## The Amazon Bedrock Converse API
Each model provider has its own native request format for `InvokeModel`. The Converse API (`Converse` and `ConverseStream`) offers one consistent message format across the models that support it.
- A message has a `role` and a list of **content blocks**.
- Block types include `text`, `image` (image bytes with a format such as PNG or JPEG, or an S3 location for some models), `document` and, for some models, `video`.
- The same request structure works when you switch between supported multimodal models, as long as that model supports image input.
## Example
One user message containing a `text` block ("What defects do you see?") and an `image` block with the photo bytes can be sent to different vision-capable models by changing only `modelId`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Converse API with image and text content blocks (correct):** one API and one message format carry both inputs together to any supported multimodal model, which is exactly the provider-independent single call required.
- ✗ **B. Separate APIs per provider:** this means maintaining different request formats per provider and splitting inputs the model needs to see together.
- ✗ **C. Upload the image to a public website:** it exposes possibly sensitive data publicly, and models called through Bedrock do not fetch images from arbitrary web URLs.
- ✗ **D. Convert the image to a long text description:** this loses visual detail the model could use, adds a separate captioning step and uses many more tokens.

## Key idea
For one provider-independent multimodal call, send text and image content blocks through the Bedrock Converse API.
Q002981:
## Designing for model service failures
Any remote dependency can be slow, throttled or unavailable. Graceful degradation means the application keeps working at reduced quality instead of failing.
- **Retries with exponential backoff and jitter**: handle brief throttling; AWS SDK retry modes `standard` and `adaptive` do this.
- **Circuit breaker**: after repeated failures the breaker "opens" and calls stop for a cool-down period, then a few test calls check for recovery. This avoids piling load on a failing service and wasting time on requests that will fail.
- **Fallback**: when a call fails or the breaker is open, return a cached answer, a simpler message ("Summaries are temporarily unavailable"), or route to an alternate model or Region, for example with a Bedrock cross-Region inference profile.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Fallback response or alternate model (correct):** users still get a useful, if reduced, result when the primary model call fails.
- ✗ **B. Crash the application:** crashing turns a partial outage into a full one for every feature, the opposite of degrading gracefully.
- ✗ **C. Block all requests until engineers act:** this makes the whole feature unavailable and waits on manual action instead of automatic handling.
- ✗ **D. Infinite retries with no delay:** immediate endless retries add load to an already failing service, exhaust client resources and can worsen throttling.
- ✓ **E. Circuit breaker (correct):** it stops sending requests to an endpoint that keeps failing, preventing cascading failures and letting the service recover.

## Key idea
Degrade gracefully with a circuit breaker to stop hammering a failing service and a fallback to keep serving users.
Q002982:
## Private hybrid connectivity to AWS
On-premises applications reach a VPC privately in two main ways:
- **AWS Direct Connect**: a dedicated network connection from your data center to AWS, with consistent bandwidth and latency.
- **AWS Site-to-Site VPN**: IPsec tunnels over the internet to a virtual private gateway or transit gateway; quick to set up and often used as backup for Direct Connect.
## Reaching the GenAI service
Once traffic arrives in the VPC, it goes to the service privately: an internal load balancer or API in the VPC, or an interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock such as `com.amazonaws.<region>.bedrock-runtime`. On-premises DNS can resolve the endpoint's private name through a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Public S3 bucket for requests:** a public bucket exposes request data to anyone, and upload-then-poll is slow and fragile compared with a direct API call.
- ✓ **B. Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN into the VPC (correct):** both provide private connectivity from the data center into the VPC hosting the service, so requests do not travel as plain public internet traffic to a public endpoint.
- ✗ **C. Email requests processed manually:** email is neither private application connectivity nor automated; it adds hours of delay and human handling of data.
- ✗ **D. Public internet with the API key in the query string:** traffic uses the public internet, and keys in URLs are logged by proxies and servers, making leaks likely.

## Key idea
For private on-premises access to a service in AWS, connect the data center to the VPC with Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN.
Q002983:
## Agents acting on behalf of users
When an agent calls a SaaS API such as a calendar or CRM for a specific user, it should use that user's own delegated permission, not a shared all-powerful key. The standard mechanism is OAuth 2.0: the user consents once, and the agent receives a token limited to that user and the approved scopes.
## Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Identity handles this for agents:
- Gives each agent a workload identity and validates inbound callers, for example with JWTs from your identity provider.
- Offers OAuth 2.0 credential providers for third-party services, including the user-consent (authorization code) flow.
- Stores tokens and API keys in a secure token vault, per user and agent, so agent code requests a token at run time instead of handling secrets.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Root credentials in environment variables:** root user credentials are AWS account credentials, not SaaS OAuth tokens, and using them in an application breaks basic security practice.
- ✗ **B. Public endpoint with no authentication:** anyone could call it, and it provides no way to act as a specific user with that user's consent.
- ✗ **C. Shared API key in the prompt:** one key gives every user the same access regardless of their consent, and a key in the prompt can be exposed through model output or logs.
- ✓ **D. AgentCore Identity (correct):** it manages user-delegated OAuth consent and tokens for third-party services, so each call acts with that specific user's permissions.

## Key idea
For per-user OAuth access to third-party APIs from an agent, use AgentCore Identity rather than shared keys or broad credentials.
Q002984:
## Troubleshooting knowledge base ingestion
A sync in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases runs as an ingestion job that reads the data source, parses and chunks documents, creates embeddings and writes them to the vector store. When some documents fail, the job itself records why.
- `GetIngestionJob` (and the sync history in the console) shows statistics such as the number of documents scanned, indexed and failed, plus failure reasons.
- Knowledge base logging can deliver per-document status to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose.
## Common causes
- Unsupported file type or a file over the size limit.
- A malformed `.metadata.json` file.
- Missing permissions for the service role on the S3 bucket, KMS key or vector store.
- Embeddings model throttling or vector store errors.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Front-end code in the browser console:** the chat UI only sends queries; document ingestion runs in the knowledge base service and never passes through the browser.
- ✗ **B. Route 53 records for the public domain:** ingestion reads from the data source over AWS service connections, not through the company's public DNS names.
- ✓ **C. Ingestion job failure details and logs (correct):** they identify which documents failed and the reason, which points directly to the fix.
- ✗ **D. Generation temperature and top P:** these affect how answers are written at query time and play no part in parsing or embedding documents during ingestion.

## Key idea
When ingestion reports failed documents, start with the ingestion job's failure details and logs, not query-time or front-end settings.
Q004430:
## How cross-Region inference interacts with SCPs
An inference profile lets Amazon Bedrock route a request to one of several Regions to get more throughput. The caller invokes the profile from its own Region, but the model can actually run in another Region of the profile's geography (for example an `eu.` profile spans EU Regions).
An SCP that keys on `aws:RequestedRegion` is evaluated for the Regions involved in the request. If the destination Regions are not allowed, the call is denied even though the source Region is allowed.
## Data residency angle
A geography-scoped profile keeps inference inside a defined geography, which satisfies an "EU only" rule. A profile that can route worldwide does not.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. The SCP is doing its job but is too narrow for the profile (correct):** the profile may serve the request from another EU Region that the SCP denies. Allowing exactly the EU Regions the profile uses restores access and still blocks every non-EU Region, so residency is preserved and the guardrail stays central.
- ✗ **B. Permissions boundary only:** a boundary is per role, so removing the SCP loses the organization-wide guarantee. Any new role without the boundary could call other Regions, and it does not fix how the profile routes.
- ✗ **C. Global profile:** a global profile can route to Regions outside the EU, which breaks the data-residency requirement the SCP was written to enforce.
- ✗ **D. Endpoint policy:** a VPC endpoint policy is a separate control and cannot override an SCP deny. SCP and endpoint policy are both evaluated, and the SCP deny still wins.

## Key idea
SCPs that restrict Regions must also allow every Region a cross-Region inference profile can route to, and geography-scoped profiles keep inference inside the required boundary.
Q004431:
## Two separate questions: content and immutability
- **Content**: which service records the prompt and response text? Model invocation logging does. CloudTrail records API calls (who, when, which model) but not the prompt text.
- **Immutability**: can anyone with admin rights change the record? A retention setting alone does not stop a privileged user from deleting data. A write-once-read-many (WORM) control does.
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode prevents any user, including the root user, from overwriting or deleting a locked object version until the retention period ends.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** Object Lock in compliance mode gives the WORM guarantee for the retention period, invocation logging supplies the prompt and response content, and Athena provides the investigation queries over the stored objects.
- ✗ **B. CloudWatch Logs retention:** a retention period expires old events, but a principal with the right IAM permissions can still delete the log group or streams, so it is not tamper-proof.
- ✗ **C. CloudTrail only:** CloudTrail records that InvokeModel was called and by whom, but not the request and response bodies, so it cannot serve as prompt-level evidence.
- ✗ **D. Versioning and Glacier:** versioning and a bucket policy can be changed or bypassed by an administrator, and lifecycle tiering does not stop deletion. Nothing enforces immutability.

## Key idea
Use invocation logging for prompt content and S3 Object Lock in compliance mode when records must be immutable for a fixed retention period.
Q004432:
## Registry approval status as a control point
Each model version in the SageMaker Model Registry is a model package with an approval status such as `PendingManualApproval`, `Approved` or `Rejected`. Changing that status is an API action, so IAM can limit who is allowed to do it.
Deployment automation can watch for the status-change event through Amazon EventBridge and deploy only when a package becomes `Approved`.
## Separation of duties
The person who builds a model should not be the person who signs it off. Enforcing this in IAM makes it a technical control that an audit can verify, instead of a convention.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automatic approval:** a metric threshold is a useful quality gate but it is not the independent model risk review that the policy requires, and it removes the human approver.
- ✗ **B. Self approval with tags:** the data scientists would approve their own work, which is exactly the conflict the policy forbids, and a tag is descriptive rather than a control.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Limiting the approval action to the risk team makes approval an independent step, and gating the production pipeline on the Approved status ties deployment to that decision. The registry also keeps the approval history for the auditors.
- ✗ **D. Spreadsheet:** it sits outside the registry, can be edited by anyone with access, and cannot be enforced by the pipeline in a tamper-evident way.

## Key idea
Enforce separation of duties by allowing only the approver role to change SageMaker Model Registry approval status and by deploying only on the Approved event.
Q004433:
## Draft versus version
In Bedrock Prompt Management the working draft is mutable: any edit changes what an unversioned reference will use. A version is a numbered snapshot of the prompt that cannot be modified afterwards.
## Why the version id matters
For evidence, three facts must line up: which prompt text existed, which version production used, and which request used it. Referencing a numbered version and logging that identifier with each request gives a verifiable chain.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Environment variable:** it does version the text with deployments, but it bypasses the prompt management catalog, offers no review history of the prompt itself, and still needs the identifier logged per request.
- ✗ **B. Screenshots:** a screenshot is manual, can be missed, and does not prove which text production actually used at runtime.
- ✗ **C. Logging only:** invocation logging can capture the rendered prompt, but relying on it alone provides no governed prompt catalog and depends on logging being enabled at that time. It also does not identify which approved prompt version was intended.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** An immutable version freezes the prompt text, pinning production to it removes silent changes, and logging the identifier with each request lets the team map any letter back to its exact prompt.

## Key idea
Reference immutable numbered prompt versions in production and log the version id with each request so any output can be traced to its prompt.
Q004434:
## Shared responsibility for compliance
AWS is responsible for compliance of the cloud infrastructure and eligible services, and publishes evidence for it. The customer is responsible for how it configures and uses those services, and must produce its own evidence.
- **AWS Artifact** is the self-service portal for AWS audit reports (for example SOC reports) and for reviewing and accepting agreements such as a business associate agreement.
- **CloudTrail and AWS Config** record API activity and resource configuration history, which is the customer's evidence of its own controls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. CloudTrail and Config (correct):** they provide the company's own configuration and activity trail, so together the two cover both halves of the shared responsibility.
- ✗ **B. Trusted Advisor:** it gives best-practice recommendations, not a compliance certification, and passing its checks does not make a workload HIPAA compliant.
- ✗ **C. Model card:** a provider's model documentation describes the model, not the customer's own risk assessment and approvals, which the company keeps in its own records such as SageMaker Model Cards.
- ✗ **D. Marketplace:** the business associate agreement is accepted through AWS Artifact, not purchased per model as a subscription.
- ✓ **E. AWS Artifact (correct):** it answers what AWS attests and lets the company accept the agreement.

## Key idea
Use AWS Artifact for AWS attestations and agreements, and CloudTrail plus AWS Config for the customer's own control evidence.
Q004435:
## Data lineage and erasure
Personal data used for fine-tuning can influence the resulting model. There is no supported way to surgically delete one person's contribution from trained weights, so the practical response is to retrain from a corrected dataset.
To do that, the team must know which datasets fed which training runs and which model versions came out. That is data lineage, and it must be recorded when training happens, for example through SageMaker lineage tracking, registry metadata or model card training details.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Editing weights:** there is no reliable procedure to subtract one record's influence from weights, and documenting an unverifiable edit would not satisfy an audit.
- ✗ **B. Output masking:** guardrails mask text at inference but the data would still be embedded in the models, and masking a name does not answer the erasure request.
- ✗ **C. Deleting objects only:** it leaves the trained models untouched and the claim that weights are never personal data is not something a controller can assume. Regulators may treat memorized data as in scope.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** With lineage, the team can list the model versions built from datasets containing the transcripts, retrain them from a filtered dataset and retire the old versions. Without it, the answer is unknowable.

## Key idea
Record dataset to training job to model version lineage at training time so erasure and provenance questions can be answered and affected models retrained.
Q004436:
## The EU AI Act in one paragraph
The EU AI Act sorts AI systems by risk. Uses such as employment and worker management are treated as high-risk. Providers and deployers of high-risk systems are expected to have, at a conceptual level, a risk management process, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping through logs, transparency to users, human oversight and appropriate accuracy and robustness.
## What it does not say
It does not require a particular hosting Region, and it does not let a cloud provider take over the deployer's own duties.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Mandatory EU hosting:** data-protection and residency rules may drive Region choices, but the AI Act does not mandate EU hosting for all high-risk systems.
- ✗ **B. No logging:** the opposite is true. Record-keeping is an expectation for high-risk systems, and privacy is handled through minimization and access control rather than by removing all records.
- ✓ **C. Human oversight (correct):** it keeps a person able to override the ranking, and can be implemented with services such as Amazon A2I.
- ✗ **D. Transferred obligations:** shared responsibility splits security tasks between AWS and the customer. Regulatory duties of a deployer stay with the deployer.
- ✓ **E. Logs and documentation (correct):** they support traceability and audits, and can be built with invocation logging and SageMaker Model Cards.

## Key idea
For high-risk AI uses, think logs plus technical documentation and real human oversight, not a mandated Region or a transfer of duties to the cloud provider.
Q004437:
## What Amazon A2I does
Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) lets you build human review workflows for machine learning predictions. You define a flow definition with a work team (private employees, a vendor, or a public workforce) and a task template. Your application calls `StartHumanLoop` when a condition is met, and A2I collects the reviewer's decision.
Built-in task types exist for Amazon Textract and Amazon Rekognition, and a custom task type supports any model, including an FM.
## Triggers
Conditions such as low confidence or a business rule can start a loop, and a random percentage can be sampled for quality audits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A2I with a custom task type and a private workforce provides reviewer tasks, decision capture and an auditable record. The application decides when to call it, which covers guardrail, amount and random sampling triggers.
- ✗ **B. Slack emoji:** it has no structured task, no controlled workforce and no dependable audit record of who approved what.
- ✗ **C. Public workforce:** customer dispute data is sensitive and the bank wants trained employees, so a public workforce is inappropriate.
- ✗ **D. Higher guardrail strength:** a guardrail is an automated control. It does not replace the human review the policy requires, and a stricter filter cannot judge disputes.

## Key idea
For human review of FM output, use Amazon A2I with a custom task type, a private workforce and application-defined triggers, including random sampling.
Q004438:
## Two human-in-the-loop options in Bedrock Agents
- **User confirmation** asks the end user of the agent to confirm or deny an action before the agent runs it. It suits cases where the person chatting is the right approver.
- **Return of control** hands the function call details back to the application instead of running a Lambda function. The application decides how to run it, including routing it to other people, then returns the results so that the agent continues.
## Choosing
When the approver is a different person and the wait is long, the workflow belongs in the application, which can persist state and wait.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Prompt instruction:** a prompt is not an enforced control, and the model can be manipulated to ignore it, so cancellation authority would still rest on model behavior.
- ✗ **B. User confirmation:** it asks the customer, who is not the licensed approver the policy requires. It is right for end-user consent, not for internal authorization.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Return of control lets the application run its own approval workflow with the right approver and time budget, then resume the agent with the result, while the agent never executes the cancellation directly.
- ✗ **D. Longer Lambda timeout:** Lambda's maximum duration is 15 minutes, which an approval can easily exceed, and holding a function open for a human is fragile and costly.

## Key idea
Use user confirmation when the chat user should approve, and return of control when another person or process must authorize before the action runs.
Q004439:
## Explainability limits of foundation models
An FM produces text token by token. When asked to explain itself, it generates a fluent justification, but that text is not a readout of the internal computation. Research shows written reasoning can omit or misstate the real drivers of an output.
## What to do instead
For decisions that affect people, keep the decision logic in auditable components (a rules engine or a tabular model with feature attributions from SageMaker Clarify) and use the FM to phrase the verified factors. Provide evidence such as source citations that the reader can check.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** The reasoning text cannot be trusted as the true cause. Grounding the explanation in the factors that actually drove the decision makes it verifiable and defensible to the regulator.
- ✗ **B. Self-rated confidence:** a confidence number the model writes is generated text too. It does not measure whether the explanation matches the computation.
- ✗ **C. Reasoning as official:** fluent step-by-step text does not guarantee faithfulness, which is precisely the regulator's concern.
- ✗ **D. Bigger model:** larger models write more fluent explanations, but size does not make them faithful.

## Key idea
Model-written explanations are not proof of the real cause. Base regulated explanations on verifiable factors and evidence, with the FM only phrasing them.
Q004440:
## Model changes are behavior changes
A new model version changes wording, refusals, tone and failure modes even for the same prompt. Public benchmarks are averages and rarely reflect a company's languages, customers and risk tolerances.
## Responsible migration
- Keep a **golden dataset** that represents real traffic, sliced by language and segment, plus a **red-team set** of adversarial cases.
- Run **Bedrock model evaluation** (automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge or human review) on both models and compare per slice.
- Roll out gradually with a canary and monitor guardrail intervention and feedback signals.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Latency and cost only:** those metrics matter for operations, but they do not measure bias, toxicity or quality, and equal quality across versions is not guaranteed.
- ✗ **B. Trust the announcement:** public benchmarks say nothing about this company's languages and segments, so regressions could reach every customer at once.
- ✗ **C. Guardrail only:** guardrails filter content but do not equalize quality, tone or correctness, and different models trigger them differently.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** A slice-level comparison on representative and adversarial data catches regressions that averages hide, and the canary limits exposure while production monitoring confirms the result.

## Key idea
Treat every model migration as a behavior change: evaluate per slice on golden and red-team data, then canary and monitor.
Q004441:
## Red teaming as a continuous process
Red teaming means probing a system with adversarial input to find failures before real users do. A one-time exercise ages quickly, because prompts, models, guardrails and attack techniques change.
## Practical shape
- A versioned suite of test cases, including multi-turn and multilingual cases, run in CI against every change.
- Release gates with thresholds.
- A feedback loop so that new real-world incidents become permanent test cases.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One-time exercise:** prompts, models and guardrails change often, so a single report stops being valid soon after launch.
- ✓ **B. Feedback loop (correct):** feeding field findings into the suite keeps the tests realistic, so together they turn red teaming into a lasting control.
- ✗ **C. Provider benchmarks:** they describe the base model in general, not this application, its prompts and its languages, so they are not evidence for this system.
- ✗ **D. Blocked prompts only:** that set contains only attacks the guardrail already stops, so it cannot reveal the ones that get through.
- ✓ **E. Automated gated suite (correct):** it catches regressions on each change to the model, prompt or guardrail.

## Key idea
Make red teaming continuous: a versioned adversarial suite gating every change, fed by production findings.
Q004442:
## Escalation is a design requirement
Even with guardrails and evaluation, harmful output will sometimes reach users. Responsible AI practice includes being able to respond quickly and consistently.
## Ingredients
- **Runbook**: severity tiers, named owners and who decides to disable the feature.
- **Traceability**: feedback linked to the invocation id in the logs, so the exact prompt, response and versions can be found.
- **Kill switch**: a feature flag, for example with AWS AppConfig, that moves traffic to a fallback such as a static answer or human agent without a deployment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Expanding denied topics:** it can be part of the fix, but without owners, a process and a way to disable the feature quickly, containment still depends on people improvising.
- ✗ **B. Email and manual log reading:** no severity process, no request linkage, and searching all logs by hand is slow and error-prone.
- ✗ **C. Quarterly sampling:** it is useful for trend review but it is far too slow for containing an incident and does not connect individual reports to the requests.
- ✓ **D. (correct):** The runbook removes hesitation, the request id shortens investigation from hours to minutes, and the flag stops the harm while the root cause is worked out.

## Key idea
Prepare escalation before launch: a runbook with owners, feedback linked to request ids, and a feature-flag kill switch to a safe fallback.
Q004443:
## Bias can drift after launch
Bias metrics measured on training data can change once the model sees live traffic whose mix of people or behavior differs. Monitoring must therefore be continuous.
## The AWS mechanism
SageMaker Model Monitor with Clarify supports bias drift monitoring: endpoint data capture feeds a scheduled job that recomputes bias metrics for the configured facets and compares them with a baseline, and violations can raise CloudWatch alarms.
Guardrails filter text content and do not measure statistical fairness of decisions.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CPU and latency:** these are operational metrics unrelated to demographic outcome balance.
- ✗ **B. Guardrail interventions:** they count blocked content, not group-level outcome rates, and could stay flat while approvals diverge.
- ✓ **C. (correct):** Bias drift monitoring recomputes group fairness metrics on live data on a schedule and compares against the baseline, so divergence in approval rates raises an alarm for the risk team.
- ✗ **D. One-time pre-training report:** it describes the historical dataset and cannot show how live behavior changes after deployment.

## Key idea
Use SageMaker Model Monitor with Clarify bias drift monitoring to watch group fairness metrics in production and alarm on divergence.
Q004444:
## What fairness evaluation needs
Public datasets are useful for a first screening, for example toxicity and stereotyping benchmarks. Fairness for a specific application depends on its users, languages and workflows, so evidence must come from data that represents them.
## Paired (counterfactual) prompts
Two prompts that are identical except for a demographic attribute let you check whether the answer quality or tone changes. Comparing scores per language and segment shows gaps that an overall average hides.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. (correct):** A custom, representative dataset with paired prompts and slice-level comparison tests the actual workflow and users. Bedrock model evaluation supports custom prompt datasets with automatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge and human review.
- ✗ **B. Self-generated tests and self-judging:** the same model creates and grades the cases, which can miss its own blind spots, and no human sampling validates the judge.
- ✗ **C. English general knowledge:** it ignores Spanish speakers and the billing-dispute domain, so it cannot reveal gaps that affect them.
- ✗ **D. Toxicity only:** toxicity is only one aspect. A low score says nothing about differences in helpfulness or outcomes between groups.

## Key idea
For fairness evidence, use a representative custom dataset with paired prompts and per-slice comparison, not only generic public benchmarks.
Q004445:
## How guardrails work with streaming
When you call a streaming API with a guardrail, the guardrail must evaluate text that arrives in pieces. Bedrock offers two stream processing modes.
- **Synchronous** mode buffers response chunks and evaluates them before they are released to the client. Nothing unscreened is shown, but the first tokens appear later and the flow is less smooth.
- **Asynchronous** mode releases chunks to the client immediately while the guardrail evaluates in parallel. Latency is best, but a chunk can be displayed before the guardrail decides to block or mask it.
The choice is a direct trade-off between responsiveness and the guarantee that no unscreened text reaches the user.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Async with exposure accepted:** this is a correct description of asynchronous mode, but it accepts the very risk the security team wants eliminated, so it does not satisfy the stated requirement.
- ✓ **B. Synchronous processing (correct):** it holds each chunk until the guardrail has evaluated it, so a disallowed answer or an unmasked account number never reaches the widget. The cost is a slower time to first token, which is the compromise the security team is asking for.
- ✗ **C. Async described as buffering:** asynchronous mode is the low-latency mode that does not wait; describing it as holding everything until the end reverses what the two modes do.
- ✗ **D. No stream processing:** guardrails do support streaming responses in both modes, and the base model's safety training does not enforce company-specific rules such as account-number masking.

## Key idea
Synchronous stream processing screens before display at the cost of latency; asynchronous is faster but may show a chunk before the guardrail intervenes.
Q004446:
## Contextual grounding outside Bedrock invocations
The `ApplyGuardrail` API evaluates text against a guardrail without invoking a model, so it works with self-hosted models and third-party APIs. The contextual grounding check compares an answer with reference material, so the guardrail needs to know which text plays which role. In the request, content blocks carry qualifiers: the reference text is the grounding source, the user's question is the query, and the generated answer is the content to guard. The guardrail then produces grounding and relevance scores and applies the configured thresholds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Unmarked concatenation:** without qualifiers the guardrail cannot tell what is reference and what is answer, so it cannot compute grounding; the service does not infer the roles.
- ✗ **B. Header on a self-hosted endpoint:** a guardrail is not attached to arbitrary endpoints; the application must call ApplyGuardrail or use Bedrock invocation APIs to get evaluation.
- ✓ **C. ApplyGuardrail with qualified content (correct):** the passages are supplied as the grounding source, the question as the query, and the answer as the guarded content, so the grounding and relevance checks have all three inputs and the response tells the application whether to block.
- ✗ **D. Comprehend sentiment:** sentiment scores say nothing about whether claims are supported by passages, and they are not what grounding checks use.

## Key idea
Use ApplyGuardrail with grounding-source, query and guarded-content qualifiers to get contextual grounding checks for models outside Bedrock.
Q004447:
## Why input tagging matters
A prompt attack (jailbreak or prompt injection) is text supplied by a user that tries to override instructions. A combined prompt mixes trusted text (your instructions) with untrusted text (user input). To evaluate only what should be scrutinised, guardrails use tagged input: with `InvokeModel` you wrap the user content in tags that carry a suffix, and with the Converse API you mark it as guard content. The prompt attack filter checks the tagged user input, not your own system instructions. If nothing is tagged, no prompt attack detection happens on the prompt. A random per-request tag suffix also stops attackers from closing the tag early.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Missing input tags (correct):** the request contains no marked user text, so the prompt attack filter has nothing to evaluate. ApplyGuardrail worked because the tester passed the attack text explicitly as the content to evaluate.
- ✗ **B. Temperature:** sampling temperature affects model output randomness, not whether the guardrail evaluates the prompt.
- ✗ **C. Numbered version:** a numbered guardrail version contains the full configuration, including the prompt attack filter, as it was saved; versions are the recommended way to deploy.
- ✗ **D. System prompt only:** the filter is aimed at user-supplied content; it is not restricted to the system prompt field, and the real gap is that nothing was marked as user input.

## Key idea
The prompt attack filter evaluates tagged user input; wrap user content in input tags (or guard content in Converse) and keep the tag suffix unpredictable.
Q004448:
## Tuning filters without guessing
Content filter strength (NONE, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH) controls how confident the guardrail must be before it acts, so a higher strength catches more but also blocks more borderline, legitimate text. Guardrails offer a **detect mode**: the guardrail still evaluates and returns its trace showing which filters would fire, but takes no blocking action. Teams use it to measure false positives on real or representative traffic, then adjust strengths per filter and per direction (input or output), and only then switch to enforcement.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Word filter override:** word filters are additional blocks; they do not allow-list text that a content filter rejects.
- ✓ **B. Detect mode (correct):** it gives evidence from real traffic with no user harm, letting the team lower only the filters that produce false positives while leaving compliance-relevant filters in place.
- ✗ **C. Set everything to NONE:** this removes protection for a week for the whole population, and with strengths at NONE the filters would not report anything useful either.
- ✗ **D. Single broad denied topic:** denied topics define subject areas to refuse and would not be more tolerant; one broad topic would likely block even more legitimate clinical text.

## Key idea
Use guardrail detect mode to measure false positives before changing filter strengths, then enforce the tuned configuration.
Q004449:
## Draft versus numbered versions
A guardrail has a mutable **working draft** used for editing and testing. When a configuration is ready, you create a **version**, a numbered snapshot that cannot be changed. Applications invoke a guardrail by identifier plus version; using `DRAFT` means every edit made in the console or API takes effect immediately for those callers. Production callers should pin a numbered version and promote a new one deliberately, which also gives a rollback by pointing at the previous number.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Draft as production:** the working draft is the editable copy and can be changed through the API too; using it in production is the cause of the problem.
- ✗ **B. Permanent detect mode:** this disables enforcement, removing the safety control that the tightened topics were meant to provide.
- ✗ **C. Delete and recreate:** this changes identifiers, breaks references and adds risk, and still does not separate edits from production.
- ✓ **D. Numbered versions (correct):** production is decoupled from the draft, so the team can keep editing and testing safely, and rollback is a version change.

## Key idea
